whyProgramming.title: Why Coding Is a Beautiful Gift for Your Child
whyProgramming.subtitle: It's not just about computers — it's about helping your child believe in themselves
whyProgramming.intro: No matter what your child dreams of becoming — an artist, a doctor, an engineer, or a storyteller — learning to code teaches them how to think, how to try, and how to believe they can figure things out. It builds quiet confidence, sparks imagination, and shows them that their ideas matter.
whyProgramming.point1Desc: Coding gently teaches children to break big challenges into small, friendly steps — a skill that helps them in school, at home, and in every part of life.
whyProgramming.point2Desc: When children code, they become creators — making games, stories, apps, and robots. Screen time becomes something magical: a canvas for their imagination.
whyProgramming.point3Desc: Through puzzles and code, children build stronger thinking skills, better reasoning, and a love for discovering how things work.
whyProgramming.point4Desc: Technology touches every dream. Whether your child loves art, nature, sports, or science — these skills will walk beside them into whatever future they choose.

faqs.question: Does my child need coding experience?
faqs.answer: The early levels introduce thinking skills through stories, play and guided activities. Children with experience can explore a later starting level based on what they can demonstrate.

faqs.question: Does every child follow the same timeline?
faqs.answer: The five levels describe a progression of skills, not a fixed calendar. Readiness for the next level depends on the child’s work and the support they still need.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a level and a course?
faqs.answer: A level describes the skills your child is practising. A course provides activities in a subject such as coding or robotics. Open a level to see its goals and the learning experiences currently listed.

meta.name: Explorer
meta.tagline: From Playful Instinct to Structured Thinking
meta.desc: A foundational journey that turns your child's curiosity into clearer thinking: sequencing, noticing, trying, and improving — through story and guided play.

seo.pageTitle: Explorer: Coding for Kids Ages 5–8 | StemTechLab
seo.pageDesc: A foundational journey that turns your child's curiosity into clearer thinking: sequencing, noticing, trying, and improving — through story and guided play.

overview.intro1: Explorer is a foundational journey for children ages 5–8, designed to guide their natural curiosity toward clearer organization, observation, and mindful trying.
overview.intro2: The journey draws on experiences that feel close to the child's world: stories, images, pathways, small challenges, and projects they can see and explain.

rows.label: Stage
rows.value: Explorer

rows.label: Delivery model
rows.value: Live online only

rows.label: Nature of the experience
rows.value: Visual, spatial, story-based, playful, and guided

rows.label: Learning language
rows.value: Playful Algorithmic Thinking

rows.label: Growth focus
rows.value: Sequencing, noticing, trying, repairing, and improving

rows.label: Role of technology
rows.value: A supportive environment for making thinking visible and building projects, not the center of the experience

overview.closing: This journey gives children a safe space to try, notice the effect of their choices, and turn small attempts into clear projects that carry traces of their thinking.

practice.intro1: Explorer focuses on building four early thinking habits.
practice.intro2: Children are not expected to memorize the names of these habits. We observe them as they gradually appear in the child's choices, explanations, and way of approaching small challenges.

habits.name: Logical Sequencing
habits.tag: I arrange my steps
habits.body:
Children begin to notice that some things need a clear order. What comes first affects what comes next, and changing one step can change the path of a story or the result of a task.

Here, children practice organizing their thoughts before acting, instead of rushing directly into trying.

habits.name: Smart Inquiry
habits.tag: I search in a smarter way
habits.body:
Children gradually move from guessing and random trying toward more attentive searching. They begin to ask: Where should I start? What have I already tried? Which path seems clearer now?

In this way, they learn that searching is not only about trying many times. It is also about noticing, comparing, and choosing a calmer path forward.

habits.name: Cognitive Flexibility
habits.tag: I notice and fix mistakes
habits.body:
The meaning of a mistake begins to change in the child's experience. A mistake is no longer the end of the attempt. It becomes a signal that helps the child pause, notice, and understand where something needs adjustment.

Instead of leaving the task at the first difficulty, children practice adjusting the path and trying another solution.

habits.name: Iterative Improvement
habits.tag: I improve after trying
habits.body:
Children understand that the first attempt is not always the final form. They can look at what they created, notice what needs improvement, and try a clearer, better-organized version.

Here, an important habit begins to grow: learning is not completed in the first attempt; it develops through review and improvement.

meta.name: Builder
meta.desc: The stage where your child’s ideas become instructions a machine can follow — first programs, first prototypes, first robots that respond.

seo.pageTitle: Builder: Coding Classes for Ages 8–10 | StemTechLab
seo.pageDesc: The stage where your child’s ideas become instructions a machine can follow — first programs, first prototypes, first robots that respond.

overview.intro1: Builder is the stage where technology stops being something your child watches and becomes something your child instructs. Ideas that used to live in their imagination now have to be written down clearly enough for a computer to follow.
overview.intro2: The work stays visual and playful — blocks rather than typed syntax, projects rather than exercises — but the thinking underneath becomes precise. A story that skips a step will not run. A robot that turns too early has to be corrected. Children learn that being exact is not a restriction; it is what makes their idea actually work.

rows.label: Stage
rows.value: Builder

rows.label: Delivery model
rows.value: Live online only

rows.label: Nature of the experience
rows.value: Hands-on, project-based, visual programming, and guided making

rows.label: Learning language
rows.value: Visual Programming and Computational Thinking

rows.label: Growth focus
rows.value: Turning ideas into instructions, spotting repetition, and fixing what does not work

rows.label: Role of technology
rows.value: An explicit tool for creation — the child now directs it rather than only responding to it

overview.closing: By the end of Builder, your child should be able to take an idea, turn it into a simple working program or prototype, test it, notice what went wrong, and improve it — and explain, in their own words, how it works.

practice.intro1: Builder focuses on four habits that turn imagination into something that runs.
practice.intro2: Your child will not be asked to memorize these terms. We watch for them in how they plan a project, react when something breaks, and describe what they built.

habits.name: Instructional Thinking
habits.tag: I turn my idea into steps
habits.body:
A computer does not guess what your child means. It follows exactly what it is told, in order.

Here children practise breaking an idea into steps that are clear, complete, and in the right sequence — the foundation every later programming skill rests on.

habits.name: Pattern and Repetition
habits.tag: I notice what repeats
habits.body:
Children start to see that a long set of instructions often hides a short pattern repeated many times.

Recognising repetition is what leads naturally to loops, and it is the first time many children experience the satisfaction of making something shorter and smarter rather than longer.

habits.name: Debugging Confidence
habits.tag: I find what went wrong
habits.body:
In Builder, things break — and that is part of the design. A program that does not work is not a failure; it is information.

Children practise staying calm, reading what actually happened rather than what they expected, and changing one thing at a time until it works.

habits.name: Digital Making
habits.tag: I build something real
habits.body:
Every stretch of Builder ends in something that exists: a game that can be played, a page that can be opened, a robot that moves.

Making something another person can use changes how children think about quality — they begin to care whether it works for someone other than themselves.

meta.name: Creator
meta.tagline: From Working Parts to Complete Projects
meta.desc: The stage where separate skills come together into projects your child plans, programs, debugs, and improves from start to finish.

seo.pageDesc: The stage where separate skills come together into projects your child plans, programs, debugs, and improves from start to finish.

overview.intro1: Creator is the stage where your child stops practising programming concepts one at a time and starts combining them. A project now needs a plan, several moving parts, and decisions about how those parts fit together.
overview.intro2: This is also where typed code usually enters properly, most often through Python, alongside the visual tools your child already trusts. The shift matters: your child begins transferring the same logic between different environments and discovers that the thinking travels even when the tool changes.

rows.label: Stage
rows.value: Creator

rows.label: Delivery model
rows.value: Live online only

rows.label: Nature of the experience
rows.value: Project-led, multi-step, increasingly independent, with guided planning

rows.label: Learning language
rows.value: Programming Fluency and Systems Thinking

rows.label: Growth focus
rows.value: Planning, combining concepts, debugging strategically, and improving a finished piece of work

rows.label: Role of technology
rows.value: A flexible medium — the child chooses how to use it to serve the project they have in mind

overview.closing: By the end of Creator, your child should be able to plan a project, program it, debug it when it misbehaves, improve it deliberately, and explain the main technical choices they made along the way.

practice.intro1: Creator focuses on four habits that turn working parts into a coherent whole.
practice.intro2: These habits show up in how your child approaches a blank page: whether they plan, how they recover from a bug, and whether they think about the person who will use what they made.

habits.name: Programming Fluency
habits.tag: I write logic I can reuse
habits.body:
Children move from writing instructions once to writing logic that can be named, reused, and trusted — the beginning of functions.

Fluency here means your child spends less energy on how to write something and more on deciding what is worth writing.

habits.name: Data and Variables Thinking
habits.tag: I keep track of what changes
habits.body:
Real projects hold state: a score, a name, a list, a setting the user chose.

Children practise deciding what needs to be remembered, what it should be called, and what happens to it as the project runs — the quiet skill behind every app that behaves sensibly.

habits.name: Systems Thinking
habits.tag: I see how the parts connect
habits.body:
A complete project is not one long instruction; it is several pieces that depend on each other.

Children begin to hold the whole shape of a project in mind, anticipating how a change in one place ripples into another — and planning for that before they build.

habits.name: User Thinking
habits.tag: I build for the person using it
habits.body:
At this stage children start designing for someone other than themselves: a sibling playing the game, a parent opening the app.

They practise asking whether something is clear, whether it explains itself, and what happens when the user does something unexpected.

meta.name: Innovator
meta.tagline: From Following Steps to Solving Real Problems
meta.desc: The stage where your child chooses and combines technologies to tackle problems that do not come with a given answer.

seo.pageTitle: Innovator: AI & STEM Projects, Ages 11–14 | StemTechLab
seo.pageDesc: The stage where your child chooses and combines technologies to tackle problems that do not come with a given answer.

overview.intro1: Innovator is the stage where the question changes. Earlier levels ask how do I build this; Innovator asks what should I build, and which tools are right for it.
overview.intro2: Projects here are open-ended by design. Your child works with advanced Python, applied AI, game architecture, interactive web, or autonomous robotics — often combining several — and has to justify the choice. The emphasis moves from learning features to exercising judgement.

rows.label: Stage
rows.value: Innovator

rows.label: Delivery model
rows.value: Live online only

rows.label: Nature of the experience
rows.value: Open-ended, project-driven, technically demanding, with mentored decision-making

rows.label: Learning language
rows.value: Applied Programming and Technical Judgement

rows.label: Growth focus
rows.value: Selecting suitable tools, structuring larger programs, debugging systematically, and solving problems without a fixed answer

rows.label: Role of technology
rows.value: A set of options to be weighed — the child decides which technology serves the problem

overview.closing: By the end of Innovator, your child should be able to take an open-ended challenge, choose suitable tools, build a substantial project, debug it methodically, and defend the technical decisions behind it.

practice.intro1: Innovator focuses on four habits that separate someone who can follow a tutorial from someone who can solve a problem.
practice.intro2: These are harder to see from the outside than earlier habits. They show up in how your child handles being stuck, and in the reasons they give for the way they built something.

habits.name: Technical Judgement
habits.tag: I choose the right tool
habits.body:
By this stage your child knows several technologies. The skill is no longer using them — it is deciding which one a given problem calls for.

Children practise weighing trade-offs and explaining why one approach suits the problem better than another they know equally well.

habits.name: Structured Design
habits.tag: I plan before I build
habits.body:
Larger projects punish improvisation. A program written without structure becomes impossible to extend or fix.

Children practise breaking a problem into parts, deciding on the shape before writing code, and keeping their work organised enough that they can return to it a week later.

habits.name: Systematic Debugging
habits.tag: I narrow down the cause
habits.body:
In a substantial project the cause of a problem is rarely where it appears. Guessing stops working.

Children practise forming a theory, testing it, ruling things out deliberately, and narrowing the search — the same discipline that underpins scientific reasoning.

habits.name: Open-ended Problem Solving
habits.tag: I work without a given answer
habits.body:
Real problems arrive underspecified, and there is no answer key.

Children practise sitting with uncertainty, defining the problem sharply enough to start, and accepting that a first attempt is meant to be revised rather than right.

meta.name: Pro
meta.tagline: From Guided Projects to Independent Work
meta.desc: The stage where your child works independently in a chosen specialization — sustaining a substantial project from first idea to finished, documented work.

seo.pageTitle: Pro: Advanced Coding & AI, Ages 13–18 | StemTechLab
seo.pageDesc: The stage where your child works independently in a chosen specialization — sustaining a substantial project from first idea to finished, documented work.

overview.intro1: Pro is not simply a harder set of courses. It is defined by independence: your child chooses a direction, sustains work over time, and takes responsibility for the quality of what they produce.
overview.intro2: Specialization deepens here — advanced Python, AI development and evaluation, or a capstone in a chosen pathway. Documentation, technical communication, and portfolio work become part of the practice, and certification such as PCEP is available as an optional external benchmark rather than a requirement.

rows.label: Stage
rows.value: Pro

rows.label: Delivery model
rows.value: Live online only

rows.label: Nature of the experience
rows.value: Independent, specialized, portfolio-driven, with mentorship rather than instruction

rows.label: Learning language
rows.value: Independent Development and Technical Communication

rows.label: Growth focus
rows.value: Sustaining substantial work, documenting decisions, evaluating quality, and presenting results

overview.closing: By the end of Pro, your child should be able to independently design, build, debug, document, present, and evaluate substantial technical work — and have a portfolio that shows it.

practice.intro1: Pro focuses on four habits that mark the shift from student to independent practitioner.
practice.intro2: At this stage the most telling signal is not what your child can build with help, but what they finish, refine, and can stand behind on their own.

habits.name: Independent Development
habits.tag: I carry a project to the end
habits.body:
The defining challenge of Pro is not difficulty but duration. Substantial work has a difficult middle, long after the initial excitement fades.

Your child practises planning their own milestones, keeping momentum without being prompted, and finishing what they started.

habits.name: Documentation and Communication
habits.tag: I explain my decisions
habits.body:
Work that cannot be explained has limited value, whether to a teammate, a reviewer, or a university admissions panel.

Children practise recording why they built something a particular way, and presenting technical work clearly to people who were not involved in it.

habits.name: Evaluation and Quality
habits.tag: I judge whether my work is good
habits.body:
Earlier levels ask whether something works. Pro asks whether it works well — and how your child knows.

Children practise testing their own assumptions, evaluating models and programs against real criteria, and being honest about limitations.

habits.name: Specialization
habits.tag: I go deep in a direction I choose
habits.body:
Breadth gives way to depth. Your child commits to a pathway — AI, games, robotics, web, or Python — and pursues it far enough to develop genuine expertise.

Choosing a direction, and accepting what that means for the roads not taken, is itself part of the learning.

challenge.badge: Free fun activity · No account needed
challenge.title: Paper Pixel Letter
challenge.subtitle: A fun 10-minute activity you can do with paper and pencil! Discover how computers see pictures — perfect to try before your very first coding class.
challenge.step1Body: Grab a blank sheet and draw a 5×5 grid (five rows and five columns). A ruler helps, but wobbly squares work too — this is about having fun!
challenge.step2Body: Color in some squares so they form the first letter of your name, nice and blocky. Stay inside the grid — no curves, just cool square shapes!
challenge.step3Body: For each row, count how many squares you colored (0 to 5). Write those numbers down — you've just written a tiny 'program' that describes your letter!
challenge.step4Body: Show someone only your five numbers. Can they guess your letter? That's actually how computers share pictures — with clever little descriptions instead of big images!
challenge.hintBody: Think of those old video games with tiny blocky letters — they were made of little squares too! Your grid is like a handmade picture, just like the ones inside every computer font.

futureThinkersSection.title: We Don't Just Teach.
futureThinkersSection.body1: Technology is changing fast — and the most valuable skill today isn't memorizing information, it's knowing how to think, adapt, and create.
futureThinkersSection.body2: At StemTechLab, we help students develop the mindset behind innovation. They don't just learn tools — they learn how to use them with purpose.
futureThinkersSection.body3: AI is part of their future. We teach students how to use it intelligently: to explore ideas, solve problems, and build meaningful projects — not just generate answers.
futureThinkersSection.pillar1Desc: Students develop strong problem-solving and reasoning skills. They learn how to ask better questions, evaluate ideas, and think independently.
futureThinkersSection.pillar2Desc: From AI tools to modern software, students learn how to use technology as a support for their thinking — not a replacement for it.
futureThinkersSection.pillar3Desc: Students apply what they learn by creating real outcomes — from simple applications to interactive projects — building confidence and practical skills along the way.

futureReady.title: We're Not Just Teaching.
futureReady.subtitle: AI will replace millions of jobs. The children who won't be replaced are the ones who learn to think, build, and create — starting today.
futureReady.body: Every tool, app, and technology your child uses was built by someone who once sat exactly where they sit now. At StemTechLab, we don't just hand kids courses. We shape how they think. We teach them to use AI as a powerful tool — not as a replacement for their own mind. Because the real skill isn't knowing how to ask ChatGPT a question. It's knowing why the answer matters, how to improve it, and what to build with it.
futureReady.pillar1Desc: We build reasoning and problem-solving skills that no AI can replicate — the ability to ask the right questions and challenge every answer.
futureReady.pillar2Desc: We teach kids to use AI as a powerful assistant, not a shortcut for thinking. The tool works for them — not the other way around.
futureReady.pillar3Desc: From games to robots to apps — kids graduate with things they actually made. That's a builder's mindset that lasts a lifetime.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.intro: This page explains the information used to provide StemTechLab services, including the optional starting-level finder. Contact us if you need more detail before sharing information about your child.
privacy.s1Content: We collect information you provide when creating an account, such as your name, email address, and your child's age and interests. We also collect usage data such as course progress and platform interactions to improve our services.
privacy.s2Content:
We use your information to:
• Provide and personalize our educational services
• Track learning progress and recommend courses
• Communicate important updates about your account
• Improve our platform and develop new features
privacy.s2aContent: When you use the starting-level finder, submitted messages and relevant conversation context may be sent through the APIs of configured providers, including OpenAI, Anthropic and DeepSeek, to interpret input and classify learning concerns. The providers used depend on enabled features and configuration. Application rules determine the provisional level suggestion. Do not include your child’s full name, school or sensitive information. Provider retention and training practices depend on the service and account settings; contact us for current details before submitting information. You can browse courses without using the finder. Human instructors teach live classes.
privacy.s3Content: A parent or guardian should provide information for a child’s enrollment and manage related requests. Share only the details needed for the service. Contact privacy@stemtechlab.com to request access, correction or deletion of information about your child.
privacy.s4Content: Keep account credentials private and share child information only through the intended service channels. Contact privacy@stemtechlab.com with security concerns or questions about safeguards and access to records.
privacy.s5Content: We use essential cookies to keep you logged in and remember your preferences (like language and theme). We do not use tracking cookies for advertising purposes on our platform.
privacy.s6Content: If you have questions about this Privacy Policy or wish to exercise your data rights, please contact us at privacy@stemtechlab.com.

faq.title: Questions from
faq.subtitle: Answers to the things parents ask us most
faq.ce1_q: What ages are StemTechLab courses designed for?
faq.ce1_a: Our five-level learning framework covers ages 5–18. Individual courses have their own age ranges and prerequisites, so the first level is not automatically the right starting point for every child. Check the course details and discuss readiness with a teacher.
faq.ce2_q: How do you keep my child's information safe?
faq.ce2_a: Account, enrollment and learning information is used to provide the service. The level finder may send submitted text to configured AI providers. Avoid entering sensitive child information in chat, and read our Privacy Policy for processing details and how to contact us about your data.
faq.ce3_q: Can my child re-watch their classes?
faq.ce3_a: Of course! Every live session is recorded and available in your dashboard within 24 hours. Your child can revisit lessons anytime — to review a tricky concept or catch up on a class they missed.
faq.ce4_a: We offer fun, optional practice activities and mini-projects after each class to help ideas stick. They take about 15–30 minutes and are designed to feel like play, not pressure. They're encouraged but never required.
faq.ce5_q: What do the classes look like?
faq.ce5_a: Classes are live, online, and full of warmth! Your child joins a small group (up to 3 students) or a private 1-on-1 session with a caring teacher. We use interactive tools, shared screens, and hands-on activities to make every minute joyful and engaging.
faq.ce6_q: What does my child need to get started?
faq.ce6_a: Prepare a laptop or desktop computer, a stable internet connection and working audio. Software and equipment depend on the course. Our introductory robotics course uses virtual simulations; check the chosen course requirements with the team before buying equipment.
faq.ce7_q: Does my child need any experience?
faq.ce7_a: There are beginner options, while some courses require prior experience. Check the course prerequisites or use the level finder to explore a provisional starting point with a teacher.
faq.ce8_q: What if we need to reschedule?
faq.ce8_a: Life happens, and we completely understand! You can reschedule a class up to 4 hours before it starts at no extra cost. You can also pause your plan anytime — your family's schedule always comes first.
faq.ce9_q: How does the starting-level finder work?
faq.ce9_a: Describe one child in English or Arabic. The finder reuses details already shared and asks one missing question at a time about age, experience, observed readiness and support needs. Validated rules produce a provisional suggestion among Explorer, Builder, Creator, Innovator and Pro. Missing, uncertain or conflicting answers lead to clarification or teacher review. Compatible published courses may be shown when available.
faq.ce10_q: What does AI do in the recommendation?
faq.ce10_a: AI can help interpret your description and identify the concern you raised. Application rules use the readiness answers to suggest a level; AI cannot override those rules. The suggestion is a starting point for discussion, not a diagnosis or a confirmed placement. A teacher helps confirm the fit.
faq.ce11_q: Does the AI track my child's progress?
faq.ce11_a: The level finder helps you explore a starting point. It does not observe lessons or track your child’s progress. Learning records and teacher feedback are available separately in the parent dashboard when added by the team.
faq.ce12_q: Is information sent to AI providers?
faq.ce12_a: Depending on the enabled features, submitted messages and relevant conversation context may be processed through OpenAI, Anthropic or DeepSeek APIs. A message can contain personal information even though no account is required. Leave out names, school details and sensitive information. Provider retention and training practices depend on the service and account settings; contact us for details before submitting information if this affects your decision. You can browse courses without using the finder.
faq.cs1_a: We're always happy to hear from you! You can write to us through our Contact page, email contact@stemtechlab.com, or use the live chat on our website. Our friendly team responds within 2–4 hours on business days.
faq.cs2_q: What if we're not happy with the course?
faq.cs2_a: We're here to help with your refund. Refunds are returned to the registered user's bank account within a maximum of 15 days. Please contact our team to request assistance.
faq.cs3_q: Can we try a class before enrolling?
faq.cs3_a: Absolutely! We'd love for your child to experience a full class with one of our teachers — completely free, with no obligation. It's the best way to see if StemTechLab feels like the right home for your child.
faq.cs4_q: Do you have discounts for siblings or longer plans?
faq.cs4_a: Yes! Siblings get 15% off, and our quarterly and annual plans come with lovely savings. Reach out to our team and we'll find the best option for your family.
faq.cs5_q: How can I see how my child is doing?
faq.cs5_a: Your parent dashboard shows you everything — completed lessons, projects your child has built, teacher feedback, and more. You'll also receive a warm weekly summary by email so you never miss a milestone.
faq.tq1_q: Who are the teachers at StemTechLab?
faq.tq1_a: Live classes are led by instructors. Ask the team who will teach your chosen course and about their relevant qualifications, subject experience and experience working with children. A trial can help you discuss their teaching approach.
faq.tq2_q: How many children are in each class?
faq.tq2_a: We keep our groups small — no more than 3 children per teacher — so every child gets the attention they deserve. We also offer private 1-on-1 sessions for children who thrive with individual support.
faq.tq3_q: Can my child stay with a teacher they love?
faq.tq3_a: Of course! When a child bonds with a teacher, that connection is precious. Just let us know your preference, and we'll do our very best to keep them together.
faq.tq4_q: How do teachers adapt to different children?
faq.tq4_a: Every child learns differently, and our teachers are trained to see that. They use a mix of visual, hands-on, and conversational approaches — meeting each child where they are and helping them shine in their own way.

guide.intro: Live online coding, robotics and AI for children ages 5–18. Start with what your child can do today, then choose a course with guidance from the team.
guide.finderHint: No account needed. The suggested level is a starting point for a teacher to confirm.
guide.stepsHeading: A simple way to get started

steps.title: Tell us about your child
steps.body: Share their age, experience and what they can do independently. The guided conversation asks for the information still needed.

steps.title: Understand their starting level
steps.body: Explore Explorer, Builder, Creator, Innovator and Pro. Age ranges are a guide; readiness and the support your child needs also matter.

steps.title: Try a lesson and confirm the fit
steps.body: Request a trial. The team will confirm availability and lesson details, and help you choose an appropriate course.

guide.approachTitle: Look for thinking you can see
guide.approachBody: A useful project is one your child can explain: what they tried, what went wrong and what they changed. Encourage small improvements and ask the teacher which skills they are practising next.

questions.title: Does my child need coding experience?
questions.body: No coding experience is needed for the early levels. Individual courses have their own entry requirements. Share what your child has tried so the team can help confirm a suitable start.

questions.title: What equipment will we need?
questions.body: Plan for a computer, reliable internet and a quiet space. Ask about software and device requirements for the chosen course. For robotics, check whether it uses simulations or physical equipment before buying anything.

questions.title: What should I confirm before booking?
questions.body: Confirm the teaching language, class format, lesson length, price, lesson count and absence or cancellation terms. For UAE families, confirm the time in UAE time (UTC+4). The website is available in English and Arabic; confirm the teaching language separately.

questions.title: How are privacy and AI tools handled?
questions.body: Ask which tools the course uses, how sessions are supervised and who can access any recordings. In the level finder, avoid names, school details and sensitive information. If AI assistance is enabled, messages and relevant context may be processed by the providers described in our privacy policy.

questions.title: How can I follow my child’s progress?
questions.body: Ask your child to show a project and explain one change they made. Agree with the teacher on feedback and next steps. After enrollment, the parent dashboard shows learning records as the team adds or shares them.

guide.enrolledBody: Open your parent dashboard for course details, progress and feedback when available. Use the details linked to your child’s enrollment.

q1.question: Where should my child start?
q1.answer:
You do not need to choose a course alone. The right starting point depends on your child's age, readiness, interests, previous exposure to technology, and way of thinking.

We begin by understanding how your child approaches learning, then guide you toward a starting point that feels suitable, clear, and not overwhelming.

q2.question: Is this right for my child's age and readiness?
q2.answer:
The right start depends on more than age. It also depends on your child's readiness, attention span, confidence, previous experience, and way of thinking.

We help guide your child toward a starting point that feels suitable — not too easy, not too advanced, and not overwhelming.

q3.question: Is this meaningful learning, or just more screen time?
q3.answer:
This is not meant to be passive screen time. The goal is to turn screen use into active learning: thinking, building, testing, and explaining.

Children are guided to use technology as a space for creating and problem-solving, not just watching, clicking, or consuming content.

q4.question: Will my child build and explain something real?
q4.answer:
Yes. Learning should become visible. Your child should not only watch lessons or repeat steps; they should build, test, improve, and explain real projects.

The type of project depends on your child's age, readiness, and way of thinking. For one child, it may start as a simple interactive story. For another, it may be a game, a robot action, a logic challenge, or a small app idea.

q5.question: Will this build thinking, not dependence on tools or AI?
q5.answer:
Yes. Tools and AI are used as learning supports, not as replacements for thinking. We focus on how your child asks questions, breaks ideas into smaller parts, tests solutions, finds mistakes, and improves their work.

The goal is not to memorize a tool or depend on ready-made answers. The goal is to help your child build a way of thinking they can use across coding, robotics, AI, and future technologies.

q6.question: How will I see my child's progress?
q6.answer:
Progress should be visible, not hidden inside lessons. We help parents see how their child is growing through completed projects, developed skills, trainer feedback, and clear next steps.

Parents can receive periodic learning summaries through WhatsApp or email, based on their preference. These summaries may include what the child worked on, what skill was practiced, what was improved, and what the next recommended step is.

Your child's progress is not measured only by attendance. It is shown in what they can build, explain, improve, and apply in new challenges.

q7.question: Who will guide my child?
q7.answer:
Your child is guided by trained educators who support learning step by step. They help children ask questions, understand mistakes, build projects, and improve their work.

The teacher's role is not only to explain, but to guide the child's thinking.

q8.question: What if the course is too easy or too difficult?
q8.answer:
The right level should feel challenging, but not overwhelming. We consider your child's age, readiness, confidence, previous experience, and way of thinking before recommending a starting point.

If the course feels too easy or too advanced, the learning path can be adjusted.

q9.question: Will my child receive feedback?
q9.answer:
Yes. Feedback is part of the learning process. Children are encouraged to review their work, understand what can be improved, and try again.

The goal is not only to finish an activity, but to help the child understand how to make it better.

q10.question: How much parent involvement is expected?
q10.answer:
Parents do not need to teach the content. Your role is to support consistency, encourage your child, and stay aware of their learning progress.

We guide the learning experience, while keeping parents informed in a simple and clear way.

q11.question: What happens if my child misses a class?
q11.answer:
Missing a class should not make the child feel lost. Depending on the course format, we help the child stay on track through follow-up, guidance, and clear next steps.

The goal is to make the learning path feel continuous and manageable.

q12.question: How do you protect my child's privacy?
q12.answer:
Child safety and privacy are treated seriously. Children are not asked to share unnecessary personal information during learning activities.

Any use of photos, videos, or public learning evidence should follow clear parent or guardian consent.
